cards.claim: Layerwise (input→output) freezing order is essential for BNNs, while global and reverse-layerwise orderings fail or collapse
cards.conditions: Full BNNs (binary weights & activations); ResNet-18/50; CIFAR-100; 200 epochs; no weight decay; constant learning rate
cards.effect: Reverse-layerwise: R18 trains to 28.4% test (collapse); R50 trains to 9.6% test (collapse). Forward layerwise: R18 reaches 53.8% test, R50 reaches 40.2% test. Gap widens with depth.
cards.evidence: Ordering ablation study with three mask progression strategies (Table 2, Figure 1); isolates effect by holding recipe constant across orderings
cards.quote: In BNNs, the ordering is decisive: layerwise training yields the best performance, global is worse, and reverse layerwise causes catastrophic collapse (Table 2). For example on CIFAR-100, reverse layerwise collapses to near-chance performance (R18: , R50: ), while forward layerwise reaches (R18) and (R50). In contrast, BWNs are far less sensitive to ordering: both forward and reverse layerwise remain competitive... These results support the interpretation that binary activations make training particularly sensitive to progression order: freezing later layers before earlier ones can severely restrict the effective learning signal reaching upstream quantized layers.

cards.claim: Binary activations with zero derivatives everywhere create gradient blockades when frozen at arbitrary depths; layerwise scheduling (input→output wave) preserves gradient paths
cards.conditions: Full BNNs; affects deeper networks more; affects networks with skip connections less effectively as mitigation
cards.effect: Gradient signal is 'severely attenuated or eliminated along many paths' (mechanism); effect worsens with depth and network width
cards.evidence: Theoretical analysis of backward-pass behavior; ablation showing BNNs fail under global masking while BWNs (with continuous activations) do not
cards.quote: In BNNs, freezing an activation uses , whose derivative is zero almost everywhere. If activations are frozen at arbitrary depths (global masking), gradient signal to earlier layers can be severely attenuated or eliminated along many paths, creating a gradient blockade. This issue is specific to BNNs: in binary weight networks where activations remain continuous (e.g., ), gradients can still propagate through activation layers... This motivates controlling where binarization is applied over time... StoMPP avoids blockades by binarizing layers sequentially from input to output. At any time, the network is partitioned into: (1) Frozen prefix ( ): fully binarized ( ) ; gradients to these layers are not required; (2) Transition layer ( ): partially frozen, updated by SoftRefresh toward ; (3) Unfrozen suffix ( ): fully continuous ( ) providing a gradient path from the loss to layer . This ensures the transitioning layer always receives a valid learning signal through its unfrozen entries

cards.claim: Stochastic masking (soft refresh) outperforms deterministic parameter freezing for depth-scaling in BWNs at constant learning rate
cards.conditions: Binary-weight networks (weights quantized, activations continuous); ResNet-18/50; CIFAR-100; 200 epochs; constant learning rate; no weight decay; stochastic masking resamples 1/r fraction of mask per step (r=5 default)
cards.effect: ResNet-50 BWN: stochastic masking 67.5% test accuracy vs. deterministic 65.5% test accuracy (+2.0 pp); effect is small but consistent at depth
cards.evidence: Ablation study comparing stochastic vs. deterministic masking policies under fixed architecture and recipe (Table 2)
cards.quote: Stochastic masking outperforms deterministic for BWN at depth. All models trained on CIFAR-100 for 200 epochs... [Table 2 shows] Layerwise Stochastic [R50]: 99.9 train, 69.0 test vs. Deterministic [R50]: 99.7 train, 68.4 test

cards.claim: Layerwise progressive freezing shows improved depth scaling compared to STE baseline; depth sensitivity degrades less steeply
cards.conditions: Full BNNs; ResNet-18/34/50; CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet; no weight decay; constant learning rate; minimal training recipe (no distillation, no architecture-specific modifications)
cards.effect: CIFAR-10 BNN: STE drops 77.8%→51.5% (R18→R50, -26.3 pp); StoMPP drops 80.9%→69.5% (-11.4 pp). CIFAR-100 BNN: STE drops 49.1%→26.7% (-22.4 pp); StoMPP drops 53.8%→40.2% (-13.6 pp). ImageNet BNN (R50): StoMPP 34.2% vs STE 30.8% (+3.4 pp at depth)
cards.evidence: Empirical comparison across three datasets and three depths; main results table (Table 1); controlled recipe isolates algorithmic effect
cards.quote: StoMPP substantially reduces the degradation with depth observed under STE. On CIFAR-10, STE drops from (R18) to (R50), whereas StoMPP drops from to . On CIFAR-100, STE declines from to , while StoMPP declines from to . On ImageNet, StoMPP improves over STE at depth (R50: vs. ), indicating that the trend persists beyond CIFAR.

cards.claim: Progressive freezing with layerwise scheduling exhibits non-monotonic (sawtooth) training dynamics, unlike smooth STE convergence
cards.conditions: ResNet-18/34/50; CIFAR-100; StoMPP with layerwise freezing schedule and stochastic refresh (r=5); STE baseline
cards.effect: Sawtooth accuracy oscillations corresponding to each layer's transition phase; STE shows smoother monotonic improvement; oscillation pattern visible in training curves
cards.evidence: Training curves (Figure 2b–d) showing accuracy trajectories; abstract mentions 'non-monotonic convergence'
cards.quote: We analyze training dynamics under progressive freezing, revealing non-monotonic convergence and improved depth scaling under binarization constraints... (b–d) Accuracy trajectories of CIFAR-100 on ResNets, trained with STE and StoMPP under the same training recipe. StoMPP exhibits a sawtooth pattern corresponding to progressive freezing, while STE improves more smoothly over training.

cards.claim: Freezing order sensitivity widens with network depth; deep networks are more impacted by blocked gradient paths than shallow ones
cards.conditions: Full BNNs; comparing ResNet-18 vs ResNet-50; reverse-layerwise (output→input) ordering; CIFAR-100; 200 epochs
cards.effect: ResNet-18: reverse-layerwise collapse to 28.4% (gap from forward 53.8% = -25.4 pp). ResNet-50: reverse-layerwise collapse to 9.6% (gap from forward 40.2% = -30.6 pp). Gap widens by ~5 pp from shallow to deep.
cards.evidence: Ordering ablation (Table 2) comparing forward vs. reverse layerwise; analysis in results section
cards.quote: The gap widens with depth, consistent with the intuition that blockages introduced late in the network can have a larger downstream impact in deeper models.

cards.claim: Binary-weight networks (activations continuous) are robust to freezing order (global/forward/reverse layerwise all viable), unlike full BNNs
cards.conditions: Binary-weight networks only (weights quantized, activations remain full-precision continuous); ResNet-18/50; CIFAR-100; 200 epochs; both stochastic and deterministic masking
cards.effect: Forward layerwise: 69.5% (R50). Reverse layerwise: 66.6% (R50). Global deterministic: 65.9% (R50). All within ~4 pp; no collapse like BNNs exhibit
cards.evidence: Ordering ablation (Table 2) showing BWN insensitivity to ordering, contrasted with BNN sensitivity
cards.quote: In contrast, BWNs are far less sensitive to ordering: both forward and reverse layerwise remain competitive, and deterministic masking can be effective at depth.
